explanations.explanation: Stars it is. Jesus tells John that the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches (Revelation 1:20). So the One writing to Ephesus is the One who holds them in His right hand and walks among the seven golden lampstands. I need my whole mustache just to carry ONE cookie box without a wobble.

Seals do show up in Revelation, so I see where your mind went. A scroll with seven seals appears in Revelation 5:1. But this letter opens with seven stars in His right hand. Same book, different part of the vision.

Seven trumpets are in Revelation too. Seven angels are given them in Revelation 8:2. But that's not how this letter opens. Here it's seven stars in His right hand, and I'll admit trumpets are tempting, since I'm LOUD on purpose.
It's the other way around, friend. Jesus says, "I know that you cannot tolerate those who are evil…" So Ephesus is NOT putting up with them. That's part of what He praises.
False is right. Jesus says, "I know that you cannot tolerate those who are evil…" Ephesus doesn't put up with them. And He names it right alongside their deeds, their labor and their perseverance.

explanations.answer: Tested them and exposed them as liars
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Jesus says they "tested and exposed as liars those who falsely claim to be apostles." Ephesus didn't just nod along. They checked, and the claim didn't hold up. That's a church paying attention.

explanations.answer: Let them teach the whole church
explanations.explanation: Not this time. The text says they tested those people and exposed them as liars. Nobody handed them a microphone. Ephesus did the opposite of what this answer says.

The text never mentions Jerusalem here. What it says is that they tested those who falsely claim to be apostles and exposed them as liars. That's all Jesus tells us about it, so I'll stick to that. I'm not adding a travel itinerary.
Yes. Jesus says they have persevered and endured many things "for the sake of My name." That's the reason the text gives. Many things, no growing weary, all for His name.
The text doesn't say that. Jesus says they endured "for the sake of My name." Nothing about the city's honor. The reason on the page is His name.

Close to how we all feel sometimes, but it's not what Jesus says. He says they persevered and endured many things "for the sake of My name." Their reputation never comes up. If I endured something for my reputation, I'd quit by lunchtime.

explanations.answer: They have abandoned their first love
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, "But I have this against you: You have abandoned your first love." Notice He said it right after naming all their good work. The text doesn't say more about what that first love looked like, so I won't guess at it. It's a heavy line, and He says it plainly.

explanations.answer: They have grown proud of their work
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that. What He says is, "You have abandoned your first love." Their work is the part He praises. The complaint is about something else.
The text never says this. Jesus' complaint is, "You have abandoned your first love." Nothing about their meetings. I'll keep to what He actually said.
Repent is the word. Jesus says, "Repent and perform the deeds you did at first." He also says to keep in mind how far they have fallen. So there's a way back, and He spells it out.
Rejoicing sounds nicer, I agree. But the word Jesus uses is repent: "Repent and perform the deeds you did at first." That's the instruction for Ephesus here.

Rest is a lovely word, but it's not the one in this verse. Jesus says, "Repent and perform the deeds you did at first." That's a call to turn back. Honestly, a nap sounds great right now, but it's not in the text.

Lampstand is right. Jesus says, "I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place." Earlier He tells John the seven lampstands are the seven churches (Revelation 1:20). So He's speaking to a church about its own lampstand.

A crown does show up in this passage, but it's in the Smyrna letter, where Jesus promises "the crown of life." For Ephesus, the warning is about a lampstand. Jesus says He will remove it from its place.
No altar in this verse, friend. Jesus says He will "remove your lampstand from its place." The seven lampstands are the seven churches (Revelation 1:20). The warning is about that lampstand.

True. Jesus says, "You hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate." So Ephesus and Jesus are on the same side here. The text says nothing more about the Nicolaitans in this letter, so that's all I'll say.

It's true, actually. Jesus says, "You hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate." He says it right after the hard line, as something to their credit. The text doesn't say more about the Nicolaitans here.

That's it. Jesus says, "To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God." It's a promise to the one who overcomes. And Jesus says to let the one who has an ear hear what the Spirit says.

That's a different tree. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is in Genesis 2:17. The promise here is the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God. Same garden-ish neighborhood, different tree.

You're thinking ahead, baker. Jesus does promise hidden manna to the one who overcomes, but in a later letter (Revelation 2:17). In this one, the promise is the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God. That's a good sign the story isn't over.

True. Jesus calls Himself "the First and the Last, who died and returned to life." He opens the Smyrna letter with those words. And a church facing suffering hears from the One who died and returned to life.
It's true, friend. The letter begins, "These are the words of the First and the Last, who died and returned to life." That's how Jesus describes Himself to Smyrna. It's right there in verse 8.
True. Jesus says He knows their affliction and their poverty, and then adds, "though you are rich!" Both are in the same verse. He sees the poverty, and He still calls them rich.
It's true, baker. Jesus says He knows their poverty, and then comes the twist: "though you are rich!" That's in the very same verse. Poor and rich in one sentence, and He's the one saying it.
Yes. Jesus says, "Do not fear what you are about to suffer." He doesn't hide that suffering is coming. But He tells them not to fear it.
The text doesn't tell them to run. Jesus says, "Do not fear what you are about to suffer." Nothing about leaving town. His instruction is about fear.

That's not what Jesus says. He says, "Do not fear what you are about to suffer." There's no hiding plan in the text. I'd have picked the hiding spot, though, since I spent years in a junk drawer and know a few.
Right. Jesus says the devil is about to throw some of them into prison "to test you." That's the purpose the text gives. It's a heavy part of the letter, and Jesus says it straight.
The text doesn't give that reason. Jesus says the devil will throw some of them into prison "to test you." That's the only purpose stated here. I'll stick with what's on the page.

The text doesn't say that. Jesus says some of them will be thrown into prison "to test you." Nothing about leaders being silenced. It's a heavy part of the letter, so I'll keep to what He actually says.
Faithful is the word. Jesus says, "Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life." It's a serious line. And it comes with a promise attached.
Joy is a great thing, but it's not the word here. Jesus says, "Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life." Faithful is the call, and the crown of life is the promise.

No, the word isn't silent. Jesus says, "Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life." The call is to be faithful. I tend to get LOUD, so silent would be a hard assignment for me anyway.
It's the opposite. Jesus says, "The one who overcomes will not be harmed by the second death." So the one who overcomes is NOT harmed by it. That's the promise at the end of the Smyrna letter.
False is right. Jesus says, "The one who overcomes will not be harmed by the second death." It's a promise, and it closes the letter. He says it right after the line about having an ear to hear.
